HYPOTHESIS TITLE: Repurposing teriflunomide, an approved multiple sclerosis drug, as an on-target DHODH-directed differentiation therapy for differentiation-blocked AML

BIOLOGICAL CONTEXT AND MECHANISM. Teriflunomide (original indication: relapsing-remitting multiple sclerosis; prodrug leflunomide historically approved for rheumatoid/psoriatic arthritis — approval and labeling facts are unverified prior knowledge to be checked against current regulatory labels) is proposed to reach free plasma concentrations in AML patients sufficient to inhibit dihydroorotate dehydrogenase (DHODH), the mitochondrial enzyme converting dihydroorotate to orotate in de novo pyrimidine synthesis (textbook biochemistry, outside-packet general knowledge). The claim applies only to differentiation-blocked AML contexts whose dominant residual pathology is an immature, lineage-blocked blast population: DHODH inhibition would deplete pyrimidine pools, release the maturation block, and drive terminal myeloid differentiation with cell-cycle exit. This is a differentiation endpoint, not bulk cytotoxicity and not stem-cell eradication; teriflunomide is not an established AML regimen.

SUPPORTED PREMISES.
- P1 (S4, PMID 27641501): DHODH inhibition promoted myeloid differentiation and altered disease-related endpoints in experimental AML, linking pyrimidine metabolism to the maturation state. S4 explicitly does not establish that any approved drug reproduces this at achievable exposure and selectivity — closing exactly that gap is this hypothesis's purpose.
- P2 (S2, 28416471): cytarabine-persistent AML cells were not consistently leukemia-stem-cell-enriched but depended on oxidative metabolism, showing residual disease contains metabolically defined targetable states; this motivates testing in treated-disease models without equating them with the S1 population.
- P3 (S1, 23333149): quiescent ROS-low leukemia stem cells showed BCL-2-linked OXPHOS dependency, demonstrating that AML subsets carry selective metabolic liabilities; used for selectivity framing only, not to predict teriflunomide effects on stem cells.
- P4 (S3, 30420752): venetoclax–azacitidine patient-associated TCA/OXPHOS disruption in leukemia stem-enriched cells supplies the established metabolic comparator and a pharmacodynamic biomarker template; reproducing that regimen is not a new repurposing proposal.

SPECULATIVE BRIDGES (assumptions, not evidence).
- B1: clinically achievable free teriflunomide exceeds the DHODH inhibitory threshold in blasts; the central quantitative assumption (reported high protein binding, long half-life; unverified prior knowledge).
- B2: blasts depend more on de novo pyrimidine synthesis than normal CD34+ cells, yielding a therapeutic window; indirectly consistent with S4 but unproven here.
- B3: DHODH's CoQ-linked activity means inhibition might secondarily perturb respiration in the OXPHOS-dependent S2 cells; secondary endpoint only.
- B4: differentiation may secondarily reduce leukemia stem-cell self-renewal without direct killing.

MODEL/CONTEXT SPECIFICATION. Test in three tiers: (1) maturation-blocked AML cell lines with matched non-AML myeloid controls; (2) primary AML blasts ex vivo from differentiation-blocked specimens, run in parallel with healthy donor CD34+ cells as the normal-cell comparator; (3) PDX xenografts for in vivo exposure and LSC-frequency effects. Arms: vehicle; teriflunomide; a high-potency reference DHODH inhibitor (e.g., brequinar; unverified prior knowledge) as positive comparator; uridine co-treatment; and venetoclax–azacitidine reference condition per S3 biomarkers.

MEASURED OUTCOMES AND CONTROLS DISCRIMINATING THE MECHANISM. On-target pharmacodynamics: LC-MS quantitation of intracellular dihydroorotate accumulation, orotate depletion, and falling UTP/CTP pools; the concentration–time course must co-segregate with phenotype. Differentiation endpoints: CD11b/CD14 induction by flow cytometry, morphologic maturation, EdU/Ki67 cell-cycle exit, and loss of colony-forming capacity; limiting-dilution xenograft re-initiation after ex vivo exposure to gauge LSC effects (B4). Mechanistic controls: (a) uridine add-back — a pyrimidine-depletion-driven mechanism should have rescue suppressed (UTP/CTP restored, CD11b/CD14 induction blocked); (b) genetic control — DHODH knockdown should phenocopy, inducible DHODH overexpression should rescue; (c) cross-resistance — cells resistant to the reference DHODH inhibitor should show reduced teriflunomide sensitivity if the target is shared; (d) off-target kinase test — monitor JAK3/EGFR-pathway phosphorylation (off-targets of the leflunomide metabolite at higher concentrations; unverified prior knowledge) against a kinase-inhibitor control arm; on-target differentiation should occur at concentrations below detectable kinase suppression.

FALSIFYING OBSERVATION. The proposed drug–mechanism–context relationship is disconfirmed if clinically achievable free teriflunomide fails to accumulate dihydroorotate or deplete UTP in blasts, or induces differentiation only at concentrations where kinase pathways are simultaneously suppressed, or if uridine fails to rescue, or if reference-inhibitor-resistant cells remain fully teriflunomide-sensitive — i.e., no co-segregation of pharmacodynamics, phenotype, and rescue across the dose–response.

SELECTIVITY AND TRANSLATIONAL LIMITATIONS. Plasma uridine salvage may blunt in vivo pyrimidine depletion; heavy protein binding and long half-life raise cumulative-toxicity concerns requiring the normal CD34+ comparator and label verification; AML genotype heterogeneity may restrict the responsive niche. Venetoclax–azacitidine remains the established metabolic regimen; any teriflunomide role would be niche or combinational, and no packet source supports AML efficacy.

ALTERNATIVE EXPLANATIONS. Cytostatic nucleotide stress without true maturation; off-target kinase inhibition at achieved concentrations; mitochondrial electron-flux perturbation independent of pyrimidine depletion; marker drift from culture conditions or serum pyrimidine content — each is specifically addressed by the pharmacodynamic, rescue, genetic, cross-resistance, and kinase controls above.

ranking.item: Repurposing teriflunomide, an approved multiple sclerosis drug, as an on-target DHODH-directed differentiation therapy for differentiation-blocked AML
